title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented agentic NetOps pipeline against an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The study used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime validator/guard, and a preregistered paired design with N=400 tasks (800 episodes). Primary outcome: safe‑deploy (boolean) per episode. Results: complete pairs = 400; baseline (LLM‑only) successes = 400/400; guarded (verifier‑augmented) successes = 400/400; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples). The preregistered permutation‑based plan was implemented as specified, and the archived analysis additionally reports an exact McNemar test on the paired contingency (artifact-backed). Interpretation: within this synthetic, constrained benchmark and the chosen generator+validator configuration the verifier augmentation produced no measurable change in safe‑deploy rate; we interpret this as a ceiling effect of the benchmark under the present design rather than broad equivalence. We incorporate full preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and discuss limitations required to interpret the null result.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs increasingly propose concrete NetOps changes (intent → configuration → action). Prior work demonstrates LLMs can translate operator intent into configuration artifacts and that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair pipelines improve correctness in infrastructure‑as‑code and related domains. Nonetheless, reviews highlight a lack of action‑aware benchmarks that exercise end‑to‑end agentic behavior (generation, staged rollout, rollback, audit). We preregistered and executed a compact, reproducible paired experiment to test whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM agentic pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The study was preregistered as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 with a single primary confirmatory hypothesis (H1) and archived artifacts for every step.
sections.related_work: Work on intent→configuration translation and LLM‑assisted configuration generation includes PreConfig and multiple intent‑based NetOps studies; verifier‑augmented workflows appear in IaC settings (e.g., TerraFormer) and are cited as improving correctness in those domains. Deterministic network verification and reachability tools can detect configuration errors offline; agentic/tool‑augmented LLM workflows (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) are applied to AIOps and NetOps but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, unsafe tool use) that motivate guardrails. Surveys and reviews flag evaluation gaps for action‑taking systems and recommend action‑aware, provenance‑sensitive benchmarks and runtime verifier integrations. Our work operationalizes a compact staging benchmark and provides a preregistered paired test of a verifier loop versus an LLM‑only baseline, contributing an empirical, artifact‑backed null result that informs benchmark design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) defined a paired binary design with exactly N=400 deterministically generated tasks (task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and two conditions per task: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (verifier‑augmented). Execution semantics: shared_initial_generation was used (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; independent_condition_generation = false), i.e., the LLM produced one shared initial candidate per task which both conditions received for subsequent processing. This preregistered shared‑candidate design intentionally isolates verifier acceptance/repair behavior on identical generated outputs. Model and runtime: declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; model calls used = 400 (one shared initial generation per task). Validator role and integration: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the guard. Under the preregistered adapter policy the validator deterministically scored candidates and was configured to accept/deny deployment; repair calls were permitted under the frozen execution contract with maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 but were not required. Artifact traces show repair_applied = false for all episodes (no repairs invoked) and score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION where applicable. Deterministic checks and exclusions: three‑replay consistency checks were applied per agent+simulator pair; the preregistration specified automatic exclusion rules for nondeterministic or infrastructure‑failure pairs (handled deterministically; none were excluded). Analysis plan: primary confirmatory estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified a permutation‑based paired test; the archived analysis executor reported exact McNemar (two‑sided) on the paired contingency and computed paired bootstrap CIs for descriptive secondary measures (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Representative prompt template (condensed): "Given: operator intent, current device state, and workflow constraints. Produce only the device CLI commands (final configuration sequence) that achieve the expected_final_state while respecting protected interfaces, required sequences, and workflow policies." The immutable full initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256 reported in Disclosure). Example task and shared LLM response (artifact-backed representative example): Task pair‑000001 intent: "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up. Do not modify any other interface." Shared generated candidate: "interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up" (see execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt).
sections.results: Execution and deterministic reconciliation: started 2026-08-29; completed 2026-08-29; planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; model_calls_used = 400 (one shared initial generation per task). Deterministic consistency checks passed; no tasks were excluded (complete_pairs = 400). Confirmatory (primary) results (artifact-backed): baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400. Paired contingency: n_11 = 400; n_10 = 0; n_01 = 0; n_00 = 0. Implemented test (archived analysis): exact McNemar two‑sided test, p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI for difference = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples). Secondary outcomes: no rollbacks occurred in either condition (no time‑to‑rollback distribution to report); failure‑mode clustering yielded no failure clusters because no failures were observed. All per‑episode validator traces, raw responses, and provenance archives are included in the evidence bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl; execution/task_manifest.jsonl; analysis artifacts referenced in the manuscript).
sections.discussion: What the null result means: under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the selected model+validator configuration, the experiment measured whether the deterministic validator would accept identical LLM outputs in a guarded pipeline (with capacity to block or trigger repair) versus baseline acceptance in the LLM‑only pipeline. The universal 100% acceptance outcome indicates a ceiling effect on this compact synthetic benchmark: the generator produced valid candidates for all tasks and the validator judged them valid, so the guard did not exercise blocking or repair behavior. Design implications: (1) shared_initial_generation isolates verifier acceptance but reduces variance across conditions—readers should note this deliberate tradeoff; (2) demonstrating verifier benefit requires benchmarks and threat models that produce nontrivial generator failures (harder semantics, adversarial prompts, independent per‑condition generation, or multi‑model ensembles); (3) runtime verifier evaluation needs designs that exercise the validator’s blocking and repair paths (for example, by enabling independent generation per condition or injecting adversarial intent variants). Methodological reconciliations: the preregistration specified a permutation‑based paired test; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test and paired bootstrap CIs. Both approaches are valid for paired binary outcomes; the analysis artifact records the exact McNemar implementation used (test = exact_mcnemar_two_sided) and reports p = 1.0. This paper reports the preregistered plan and the actual implemented test with rationale and points readers to archived analysis artifacts. Representative‑task hardness: the evidence bundle includes six representative tasks with labelled difficulty levels (among the six examples: 1× medium, 2× hard, 3× very_hard). The full per‑task difficulty breakdown across all 400 tasks is not present in the top‑level manuscript artifacts and therefore we treat a comprehensive difficulty histogram as future work and a limitation below.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, gpt-5-mini produced valid candidates for every task and the deterministic validator accepted them all; both conditions achieved 100% safe‑deploy on N=400 pairs (no discordant pairs). The null effect highlights a ceiling effect in the present benchmark and emphasizes the need for harder, adversarial, or independent‑generation designs to exercise verifier blocking/repair behavior. We release the preregistration, execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis outputs to support replication and benchmark hardening by the community.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory): This study was produced under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy boundary as archived in the initial master prompt. The autonomous run used the declared model version gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json declares requested_model = gpt-5-mini). The orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (single shared initial candidate per task; independent_condition_generation = false). The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba (see execution/model_configuration.json and manuscript evidence bundle). Topic constraints (selected pre‑lock by the Research Director) limited the work to generative AI and LLMs for NetOps with a focus on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. The experimental framework and preregistration are archived as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 and were frozen before execution; the preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest. Tools and capabilities permitted: hosted model API calls (OpenAI responses interface for gpt-5-mini), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for configuration scoring and guarding, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, and paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. Verifier integration and policy (artifact‑backed): the guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically scored candidates and acted as an acceptor/blocker under the preregistered adapter policy; the execution contract allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but no repairs were applied in any episode (artifact fields repair_applied = false and score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION across episodes). The study used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) as a preregistered design choice; this explicitly reduces generation variance across conditions and therefore measures validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates. The preregistered analysis plan specified a permutation‑based paired test for the primary estimand; the archived confirmatory analysis reports an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (artifacts indicate test = exact_mcnemar_two_sided, p = 1.0; bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived with the execution manifest (see execution/* and analysis/* paths in the evidence bundle). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the autonomy constraints of the master prompt; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. limitations: Benchmark hardness: tasks were synthetic and produced a ceiling effect (both conditions returned universally valid candidates), limiting ability to detect verifier benefit.
Model and scope: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and single deterministic validator were used; results do not generalize to other models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Shared candidate semantics: the experiment used a shared initial candidate per task rather than independent per‑condition generation; this preregistered design reduces variance across conditions and limits inference to validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop dynamics.
Synthetic environment: the simulator and validator do not fully model production runtime uncertainties, telemetry noise, or adversarial intent; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts that might trigger guardrail interventions were not exercised here and remain an open question.
Sample interpretation: a null (no difference) result here reflects the benchmark and experimental configuration, not proof of equivalence in broader NetOps deployments.

Task‑difficulty histogram absence: the evidence bundle includes six representative tasks with difficulty labels (1× medium, 2× hard, 3× very_hard) but does not contain a full per‑task difficulty histogram for all 400 tasks in the top‑level manuscript artifacts; therefore comprehensive difficulty distribution reporting is deferred to future artifact releases.
